study.title: 1 Samuel 2 - The prayer of Hannah, the contrast between houses and judgment on Eli
study.overview: Chapter 2 presents three main movements. First, Anna's prayer celebrates the Lord as the only saint, sovereign and judge who reverses human situations: he overthrows the strong, raises the weak, humbles the proud and exalts those who trust in him. Then the text contrasts Samuel's increasing fidelity to the corruption of Eli's sons, who despise the offerings of the Lord and profane the worship. Finally, God sends a man of God to announce to Eli that his house will be judged, because he has honored his children more than the Lord; in his place God will raise up a faithful priest.

outline.title: Ana's prayer: God is holy, sovereign, and judge
outline.explanation: Hannah does not just speak of her personal joy; her prayer interprets all the reality from who God is. He is incomparable in holiness, a refuge for his people and judge who weighs the actions. The song describes strong reversals: powerful are broken, hungry are satiated, the barren receives children, poor are exalted and history ends in expectation of a king and his anointed.

outline.title: Samuel grows before the Lord, while Eli's house is disordered
outline.explanation: The text alternates between the spiritual health of Elkanah's family and the corruption of the priestly house. Samuel ministers to the Lord, is cared for by Hannah and grows under the divine blessing. In contrast, Eli's sons practice abuse in worship and grave sin, while the Lord continues to visit Anne with other sons and daughters.

outline.title: The weak rebuke of Eli and Samuel's growth
outline.explanation: Eli knows the evil of his children and rebukes them, but his correction is insufficient in the face of the gravity of sin. The text emphasizes that they have not heard the father's voice, and this is presented as God's judgment. In the same gloomy scenario, Samuel continues to grow in favor before God and people.

outline.title: The sentence against Eli's house and the promise of a faithful priest
outline.explanation: The man of God recalls the election of Eli's house and accuses his unfaithfulness: they despised the sacrifices and honored the children above God. The sentence includes loss of authority, humiliation, and death of the descendants. At the same time, God promises to arouse a faithful priest, while what remains of Eli's house will end up asking for work and bread.

study.context: The chapter is located in the environment of the tabernacle in Shiloh, where Eli exercised the priesthood and Samuel served the Lord. The notes highlight Elkanah's house in contrast to Eli's house: on the one hand, devotion, gratitude and growth; on the other, wickedness, abuse of worship and moral corruption. The text also anticipates the replacement of the unfaithful priestly lineage by another that will please God.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that God is absolutely holy, unique and trustworthy. He rules history with justice and freedom: slaughter and exalts, impoverishes and enriches, gives life and removes it. Ana's prayer shows that God's grace reaches the humble and frustrates human pride. Verse 10 broadens the horizon by speaking of king and anointed, which can be read as real expectation and, in Christian reading, as an anticipation of the Messiah. At the same time, the chapter states that religious privilege does not replace obedience: external proximity to worship does not prevent judgment when there is contempt for God. Eli's spiritual responsibility is also highlighted; his omission contributes to the sin of his children. In contrast, Samuel appears as an example of growth in fidelity, showing that God preserves servants who honor him.

scholarViews.insight: The Iung in Anna's song is presented as a prophetic culmination point, pointing to both kings of Israel and the supreme king of God, the Messiah.
The family of Elcana and Eli's house are placed side by side so that the piety of one makes the iniquity of the other more visible, and vice versa.
The sentence of humiliation includes Eli's descendants asking for humble work and even a piece of bread, an image of the ruin resulting from his sin.

questions: How does Ana's prayer correct our tendency to think what success, strength, and position are automatic proofs of divine approval?
In which areas can we, like Eli, tolerate sin for lack of firmness, even though he knows that he dishonor the Lord?
What does it mean, in practice, to grow the Lord's "beast like Samuel," in the midst of a confused spiritual environment?
study.practice: This week, pray from Ana's model: recognize who God is before asking for anything. Also examine whether there is any area in which you have honored people, outcomes or interests above the Lord. If any, confess this and take a concrete attitude of obedience: correct an omission, treat a tolerated sin seriously, or reserve daily time to serve God reverently. At the same time, imitate Samuel's constancy: remain faithful in the place where God has placed him, even when the surrounding environment is not ideal.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the main line of the chapter, but do not authorize external details such as precise dates, expanded historical identification of the "man of God" or reconstructions beyond what the text itself says. Some commentators mention alternative readings for verse 25, but the text and notes do not require definitively resolving this issue for the present study.
